subject: Cognitive Science
title: The Sensorimotor Stage
description: A fast breakdown of The Sensorimotor Stage for builders.

hook.text: Hide a toy under a blanket and a six-month-old stops looking. Out of sight, out of mind—literally.

buildup.text: Piaget's first stage (birth to two) says babies think by doing—grabbing, sucking, shaking.

discovery.text: Around eight months, object permanence appears. The baby searches for hidden objects at last.

twist.text: But the A-not-B error lingers: hide a toy at B after hiding at A, and the baby checks A again.

climax.text: By age two, toddlers can mentally represent absent objects. Thought is no longer tied to action.

punchline.text: First you act, then you imagine acting.

quiz.question: What milestone emerges in the sensorimotor stage?

details.summary: Piaget's sensorimotor stage spans birth to about two years, when infants learn through physical interaction with objects. Babies develop object permanence, the understanding that things exist even when hidden, and progress from reflexive actions to intentional goal-directed behavior.
details.whyItMatters: This stage explains how raw sensory experience becomes organized thought. Every later cognitive achievement builds on lessons learned by reaching, grasping, and exploring.
takeaways: Lasts from birth to roughly age two
Object permanence develops during this stage
Intentional behavior replaces simple reflexes over time

faq.question: What is object permanence in simple terms?
faq.answer: Object permanence is knowing something still exists even when you cannot see it. Young infants act as though a hidden toy has vanished. By around 8 to 12 months, babies will search for hidden objects, showing they understand things persist beyond immediate perception.

faq.question: How did Piaget study infants in this stage?
faq.answer: Piaget observed his own three children in naturalistic settings, noting how they interacted with objects. He used tasks like hiding toys under blankets to test when babies would search for them, documenting the gradual transition from reflexive to goal-directed actions.
